findings.passage: The sixth Streamer Awards are scheduled for November 12, 2026, two days after this was written.
findings.problem: The page ends on a forecast that expires two days after accuracy_checked_at. "are scheduled" and "two days after this was written" will both read wrong to anyone who opens the page after November 12, 2026, and the body never tells the reader that the show testing her promised "very hard pivot" falls outside the record. The trophy-theft item that follows does no work for the type argument; it is the newest news, not evidence. Five review triggers (C17, C29, C31, C41, C48) all fire on that same date.
findings.acceptance_test: No sentence in the body or FAQs describes the November 12, 2026 show in future or scheduled tense, and "after this was written" is gone. The limits section says in one dated sentence that the record closes on November 10, 2026, before the sixth show, so the 2026 pivot is untested here. The trophy theft is either cut or tied in one clause to the argument (for example, how she takes a lost object versus a peer's disapproval). research_tasks keeps the post-November-12 update covering C17, C29, C31, C41 and C48.

findings.passage: She has also said of the people in it: "Nobody gives a shit about what's keeping me up at night."
findings.problem: The title, meta_title, opening question, the "A version of me" section and the last paragraph all stand on one sitting with GQ in December 2025, in a month she called a beating, and GQ itself called the surname-and-birthday remark hyperbolic. At first use it has no date and no source link. meta_title ("The Host Nobody Knows") drops the attribution and states it as fact. The evidence record files C28 as stable with no review_trigger, so nothing prompts a recheck if she describes those friendships differently, for instance after an October 2026 wedding attended by the same peers.
findings.acceptance_test: The first use of the quote names GQ and December 2025 and links the source. meta_title keeps the claim as something she says, as the title does. C28 is time_sensitive with a trigger such as "recheck if she describes her peer friendships differently in a later interview". The closing paragraph may keep its image as long as the reader has already been given the December 2025 date.

findings.passage: persona_title: The Host Who Pays for the Party
findings.problem: The persona label and the description ("QTCinderella pays for streaming's biggest night") state as permanent fact the claim the body treats most carefully: C17 is self-reported, unaudited and time_sensitive, and the body says the show has had sponsors. A profit, a broadcast deal after the May 2026 CAA signing, or the end of the show would make the label false. "streaming's biggest night" is a superlative with no claim in the inventory.
findings.acceptance_test: persona_title names something that stays true if the financing changes (her hosting, seating or giving), or carries the same "by her account" hedge the body uses. The description either attributes and dates the financing claim or drops it, and "biggest night" is replaced with a description the body supports. Every factual metadata claim that remains has an inventory entry.

findings.passage: By her account, no. In March 2023 she called the show a passion project
findings.problem: Several changing facts are written in open present tense with no as-of date at the sentence: this FAQ's lead answer (her last statement is December 2025); "Winners are decided 70% by public vote and 30% by a panel" in body and FAQ; "She also runs it nearly alone" (GQ, December 2025, before CAA); "GQ still calls her" small fry; "GQ reported that she struggles with dissociation"; "Five editions at a stated loss" (her statement predates the fifth show's accounts); and "She co-hosts the podcast Wine About It", which appears only in the FAQ and keywords while the body never names the podcast.
findings.acceptance_test: Each of those sentences carries its own year or "as of" date (for example "As of December 2025, by her account, no"; "for the 2025 show, winners were decided..."; "in December 2025 GQ described..."). The loss claim is bounded to what she said and when. Wine About It is either named and dated in the body with its cohost or removed from the FAQ.

findings.passage: In October 2026 the pattern ran small.
findings.problem: A three-week-old dispute gets about 130 words directly after the paragraph called the center of the Type 2 reading, but the draft never says which pattern it repeats, and it concedes the podcast audio was not reviewed and the tone is unknown. The sharpest quote in it is Ahgren's, not hers. In five years this reads as leftover news. The thesis stands without it (C37 is not in for_claim_ids), so its length should match its weight.
findings.acceptance_test: The passage either states in one clause what it shows about her (with her own words as the evidence, not Ahgren's) and stays within its stated limits, or is cut to a short dated record of the dispute, her post, the critics' point and ExtraEmily's response. Removing the paragraph leaves the section's argument unchanged.

findings.passage: She also runs it nearly alone. GQ described her as creator, producer, showrunner and talent wrangler, with one assistant and a contracted production team.
findings.problem: Evidence-record triggers have gaps. C18 (staffing) is marked stable although it describes December 2025 and she signed with CAA in May 2026. C25 (forgiveness and distance from Ewing) is stable with no trigger although the status of that relationship can change. C08 (dissociation) is a health status marked stable. C10 has a research task to open the Dr. K recording but no trigger on the claim, though the draft calls it the best single test of the Type 3 reading.
findings.acceptance_test: C18 and C08 are time_sensitive with concrete triggers. C25 has a trigger ("recheck if she and Ewing appear together or she revises the statement"). C10 carries a trigger to reopen the type argument once the June 20, 2020 recording is reviewed. No claim describing a present status is left as stable with an empty review_trigger.

findings.passage: a rerun channel she set up to fund the 2024 show got both of her Twitch accounts banned for 41 minutes on February 10, 2024, after it showed a clip that broke Twitch's rules ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QTCinderella))
findings.problem: A controversy fact with precise figures rests only on a live Wikipedia page, which can be rewritten at any time; the same is true of culinary school and the Disneyland origin of her handle. A reader or verifier in 2031 may find the cited page no longer says this. The research notes confirm no other source was opened for the ban.
findings.acceptance_test: The ban is cited to a dated contemporaneous report, or the Wikipedia link is a permanent revision link with the access date, or the precise figures (41 minutes, both accounts) are dropped. The same choice is made for culinary school and the Disneyland detail.

findings.passage: GQ's account includes a cohost's joke comparing [Kai Cenat](/personality-analysis/kai-cenat) to Diddy and claims online afterward that the jokes were racist and that streamers had acted homophobic.
findings.problem: The controversy paragraph depends on 2025 references a later reader will not have: why a Diddy comparison was a complaint, who "Fanfan" is (the cohost is never named outside the quote), and what the "Piker shock-collar jokes" refer to. Without them the named critic's argument, which the controversy standard requires, is hard to follow five years on.
findings.acceptance_test: The cohost is named once in author prose, and one short clause each explains the Diddy comparison and the shock-collar reference, with the GQ quotation left word for word. A reader with no memory of 2025 streaming news can say what the complaint was.

assessment: Five-year test: the thesis survives removal of the latest events. The Type 2 read rests on a pattern dated 2021 to 2025 across five outlets (Sh*tcamp, the 2023 Vice list, the 2025 Frost reply, the repeated wish to be understood); the October 2026 wedding dispute and the trophy theft are not load-bearing. Dating is mostly absolute and the limits section is honest. The durability problems are at the edges. The body closes on a show scheduled two days after the accuracy check, with five review triggers firing that day. The title-level claim that nobody knows her comes from one December 2025 interview, is undated at first use, and is filed as stable. persona_title and description turn a self-reported, time-sensitive financing claim into a permanent label. Several present-tense status sentences need as-of dates, and a few claims lack review triggers or rest on a live Wikipedia page. Similarity diagnostic: tripped on two pairs with olivia-dean. I compared them: one is the standard not-a-diagnosis sentence and the other is ordinary Type 2 vocabulary ("the giving goes unseen" versus "unthanked"); the arguments differ and I found no meaningful reuse, so no finding. I did not reopen sources; that is the evidence role. Risk flags: sensitive allegations (deepfake targeting, her account of childhood abuse, unproven rigging accusation, racism and homophobia complaints about the 2025 show) and contested typing (medium confidence, Type 3 live) both apply.
